steps.title: Import React and hooks from 'react'
steps.instruction: Import React, useState, and useDeferredValue from the 'react' package.
steps.hint: Use a single import statement to bring in all three from 'react'.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of importing React and hooks
import React, { useState, useDeferredValue } from 'react';
steps.seedCode: // Import React, useState, and useDeferredValue from 'react'
steps.expectedOutcome: The imports for React and the necessary hooks are added to the file.
successCriteria: The code should include an import statement that imports React, useState, and useDeferredValue from 'react'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully imported React, useState, and useDeferredValue. These are the building blocks we'll use in this lesson.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close, but check your import statement. Make sure you're importing React, useState, and useDeferredValue all from the 'react' package.
steps.feedbackWrong: That doesn't look right. You need to import React, useState, and useDeferredValue from 'react' using a single import statement.

steps.title: Create the main component
steps.instruction: Create a functional component named App that returns JSX. The component should be defined with TypeScript syntax.
steps.hint: You can use either a function declaration or arrow function. Remember to include the return type (JSX.Element) for TypeScript.
steps.seedCode:
// Import React, useState, and useDeferredValue from 'react'

// Create the App component here
steps.expectedOutcome: You'll have a functional component named App that returns JSX, ready to build upon in later steps.
successCriteria: The code should define a component named App that returns JSX (any valid JSX structure). The component must be properly defined with TypeScript syntax.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created the App component with proper TypeScript syntax. This gives us a foundation to build our useDeferredValue example.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but there might be an issue with the component definition. Make sure you've created a functional component named App that returns JSX with TypeScript syntax.
steps.feedbackWrong: The component definition doesn't seem correct. Remember to create a functional component named App that returns JSX using TypeScript syntax.

steps.title: Initialize search input state
steps.instruction: Inside your App component, use the useState hook to create a state variable called 'search' initialized to an empty string.
steps.hint: Remember to use the useState hook you imported earlier. The state variable should hold string values.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of initializing a string state variable
const [search, setSearch] = useState<string>('');
steps.expectedOutcome: You should have a search state variable that will store the user's input text.
successCriteria: The code must include a useState call that declares a 'search' variable and a 'setSearch' setter function, initialized with an empty string.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully initialized the search state variable. This will track the user's input as they type.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure you're using useState to create a state variable called 'search' that starts as an empty string.
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's try again. You need to use the useState hook to create a state variable for the search input.

steps.title: Create deferred search value
steps.instruction: Inside your component, use the useDeferredValue hook to create a deferred version of your search state. Call the result deferredSearch.
steps.hint: useDeferredValue takes a value and returns a deferred version of it. Use it with your search state variable.
steps.expectedOutcome: You should have a deferredSearch variable that holds the deferred version of your search state.
successCriteria: The code must call useDeferredValue with the search state variable and assign the result to a variable named deferredSearch.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created a deferred version of your search state using useDeferredValue.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're calling useDeferredValue with your search state and assigning the result to deferredSearch.
steps.feedbackWrong: This step requires using useDeferredValue to create a deferred version of your search state. Check that you're calling the hook correctly and naming the result deferredSearch.

steps.title: Create search handler function
steps.instruction: Inside your App component, create a function called handleSearchChange that takes an event parameter and updates the search state with the input value.
steps.hint: Define a function that receives a React.ChangeEvent<HTMLInputElement> and calls setSearch with event.target.value.
steps.expectedOutcome: You should have a handleSearchChange function that updates the search state when called with an input change event.
successCriteria: The function must be named handleSearchChange, accept an event parameter of type React.ChangeEvent<HTMLInputElement>, and call setSearch with event.target.value.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created the search handler function that will update the search state when the input changes.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check that your function: 1) is named handleSearchChange, 2) accepts an event parameter with proper typing, and 3) calls setSearch with the input value.
steps.feedbackWrong: The function doesn't meet the requirements. Make sure to create a function called handleSearchChange that takes a change event and updates the search state.

steps.title: Return the main container
steps.instruction: Update the return statement to wrap the existing content in a div with className 'app'.
steps.hint: Replace the current div wrapper with a div that has the className attribute set to 'app'.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component returns a div container with className 'app' wrapping the existing content.
successCriteria: The return statement should contain a div element with className='app' that wraps the h1 element.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully wrapped the content in a div with className 'app'. This provides a container for styling and layout.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close, but make sure the div has exactly className='app' (not class) and wraps the h1 element.
steps.feedbackWrong: The return statement should have a div with className='app' containing the h1. Check your syntax.

steps.title: Add search input field
steps.instruction: Inside the return statement of your component, add an input element with type='text', a placeholder like 'Search...', value bound to the search state, and onChange wired to the search handler function.
steps.hint: The input should be added inside the main container div, after the h1 element. Use the search state for value and the handler for onChange.
steps.expectedOutcome: The UI will show a search input field below the heading. The input will be controlled by React state.
successCriteria: The input element must have: type='text', placeholder attribute, value={search}, and onChange={search handler}.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added the search input field with proper binding to state and handler.
steps.feedbackPartial: You added an input, but check if it has all required attributes: type='text', placeholder, value={search}, and onChange={search handler}.
steps.feedbackWrong: The search input field is missing or incomplete. Make sure to add an input element with type='text', placeholder, value bound to search state, and onChange wired to the handler.

steps.title: Add current search value display
steps.instruction: Inside the return statement of your component, add a paragraph element that displays the current search state value. Use the search variable directly in JSX.
steps.hint:
Add a

tag after the search input field. Inside the paragraph, use curly braces to reference the search state variable.
steps.expectedOutcome: The UI will show a paragraph displaying the current search input value as you type.
successCriteria:
Add a

element that contains the search state variable inside JSX curly braces.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added a paragraph that displays the current search value. This shows the immediate state value as the user types.
steps.feedbackPartial:
You're close! Make sure you've added a paragraph element (

) that displays the search state value using curly braces.
steps.feedbackWrong:
The paragraph element displaying the current search value is missing or incorrect. Please add a

tag that shows the search variable.

steps.title: Add deferred search value display
steps.instruction: Add a paragraph element inside the main container that displays the deferred search value. Use the variable name 'deferredSearch'.
steps.hint:
Create a

tag with the text content showing the deferred value. For example:

Deferred value: {deferredSearch}
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of displaying a deferred value in a paragraph

Deferred value: {deferredValue}
steps.expectedOutcome: A paragraph element showing the deferred search value appears below the current search value display.
successCriteria: The paragraph displays the deferredSearch value
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added a paragraph that displays the deferred search value. This shows how useDeferredValue creates a version of the state that can lag behind the current input.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're displaying the 'deferredSearch' variable inside the paragraph. Check that you're using the correct variable name and JSX syntax.
steps.feedbackWrong:
The paragraph showing the deferred search value is missing or incorrect. Remember to add a

element that displays the 'deferredSearch' variable value.

steps.title: Create search results component
steps.instruction: Create a new functional component named SearchResults that takes a query prop of type string and returns a JSX element. Inside the component, simulate expensive filtering by creating a filtered list of items that match the query.
steps.hint: Define the component with either function SearchResults(props) or const SearchResults = (props) => {}. The query prop should be typed as string. You can simulate filtering by creating an array of sample items and using filter() with includes().
steps.expectedOutcome: A new SearchResults component is created with proper TypeScript typing for its query prop and simulates filtering logic inside.
successCriteria: The SearchResults component should be defined with a query prop of type string, contain a sample array of items, and filter those items based on the query.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created the SearchResults component with proper TypeScript typing and filtering logic. This component will simulate expensive rendering operations that useDeferredValue helps optimize.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've created a component, but it's missing some required elements. Make sure to: 1) Accept a query prop typed as string, 2) Create a sample array of items, 3) Filter those items based on the query, and 4) Return JSX that displays the filtered results.
steps.feedbackWrong: The SearchResults component is not properly defined. You need to create a new functional component that takes a query prop and simulates filtering. Check the example for the correct structure.

steps.title: Add search results to main component
steps.instruction: Add the SearchResults component to the App component's JSX, passing deferredSearch as the query prop.
steps.hint: Inside the App component's return statement, add the SearchResults component as a JSX element with a prop named 'query' set to the deferredSearch value.
steps.analogousExample:
// Adding a component with props
<SearchResults query={deferredSearch} />
steps.expectedOutcome: The SearchResults component should be rendered in the App component with the deferredSearch value passed as a prop, demonstrating how deferred values can be used for expensive rendering.
successCriteria: The learner must add the SearchResults component JSX element to the App's return statement and pass deferredSearch as the query prop.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added the SearchResults component with the deferredSearch prop. This shows how useDeferredValue can be used to pass a deferred value to components that perform expensive rendering.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're passing the deferredSearch variable as the query prop to the SearchResults component.
steps.feedbackWrong: The SearchResults component isn't properly added or the deferredSearch prop isn't passed correctly. Check that you're adding <SearchResults query={deferredSearch} /> inside the App's return statement.

steps.title: Add explanatory comments
steps.instruction: Add a comment above the deferredSearch variable declaration to explain how useDeferredValue works to defer updates for better performance.
steps.hint: Write a clear comment that describes the purpose of useDeferredValue in this context.
steps.analogousExample:
// useDeferredValue delays the update of deferredValue until after urgent updates, improving responsiveness
const deferredValue = useDeferredValue(value);
steps.expectedOutcome: The deferredSearch variable declaration now has an explanatory comment describing how useDeferredValue defers updates.
successCriteria: The code includes a comment above the deferredSearch variable that mentions useDeferredValue and its performance benefit.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've added a helpful comment explaining how useDeferredValue defers updates to improve performance.
steps.feedbackPartial: You added a comment, but it could more clearly explain how useDeferredValue defers updates for better performance. Try mentioning the performance benefit explicitly.
steps.feedbackWrong: The comment is missing or doesn't explain how useDeferredValue defers updates. Add a comment above the deferredSearch variable declaration that describes this behavior.
